name: Beeswax hair removal (ancient)

lead: Hair removal with sticky substances is among the oldest grooming practices. A layer of wax or paste is pressed onto the skin and pulled off, taking hairs out at the root, which leaves skin smooth for several weeks.

The modern descendants are strip and hard waxing and sugaring. Hair-removal history describes smooth skin as an ideal in ancient Egypt, Greece and Rome, with depilatories and attendants who removed hair for bathers.

paras: In modern waxing, wax is spread on the skin and removed with a cloth strip, or hardens and is peeled off without a strip. Regrowth is usually reported at roughly two to eight weeks. Sugaring uses a paste of sugar, water and lemon juice or honey.

Reported drawbacks include pain, ingrown hairs, red bumps, minor bleeding and cold-sore flare-ups. Skin lifting is more likely with blood thinners, autoimmune medication, steroids, recent sunburn, rosacea or topical retinoids.

angle.text: A layer of wax or paste is applied and removed with the hairs, leaving skin smooth until regrowth. Practitioners favour it over shaving for longer-lasting results.

lead: Beeswax hair removal refers to the use of wax or other sticky substances to pull body hair out at the root, a method associated with ancient grooming and continued in modern waxing. Its appearance payoff is smooth, hairless skin that lasts longer than shaving, with regrowth typically reported after several weeks.[1]

Hair removal in general is recorded from antiquity. In ancient Egypt it was common among wealthy people, and in Greece and Rome both men and women removed hair, with attendants called alipili doing so for bathers; smooth skin was linked with purity and status in Rome.[2] The sources loaded for this entry do not describe beeswax use specifically in those cultures, and the closest documented relative is sugaring, said to have been in use since about 1900 BC in the Persian region.[3]

paras: Waxing removes hair from the root by adhering a sticky layer to it and pulling. In strip waxing the wax is spread thinly and a cloth or paper strip is pulled against the direction of growth; hard or film wax hardens and is peeled off without strips, which is said to suit sensitive skin.[1]

Hair removal has been practised since at least the Neolithic era. In ancient Egypt it was common among the wealthy and was associated with controlling lice; pumice and razors were used.[2] Greek and Roman depilatories such as psilothrum and dropax are named in sources, though their ingredients are not described there, and Suetonius wrote that Augustus used hot nutshells on his legs.[2]

Sugaring, a sticky sugar-and-lemon or honey paste called sukkar or halawa in the Middle East, is described as in use since 1900 BC, and its article speculates that honey may have been the first agent.[3]

Common drawbacks are pain, cost, ingrown hairs, red bumps and minor bleeding. Skin lifting is more likely with blood thinners, autoimmune drugs or steroids, recent sunburn or surgery, rosacea, and topical retinoids or acid peels. Waxing can also trigger cold sores.[1]
